transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The fly Dubai pilots in an altercation this week that forced an emergency landing of their
plane are now in the United Arab Emirates.
The passengers aboard were mostly Israeli.
The UAE is investigating the case and potential motives, and Pierre's Ayyabhatrawi reports
from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia says the pilots left the city of Tabuk on Thursday and were flown to the
United Arab Emirates, accompanied by an Emirati security team.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the plane's captain was stabbed by his
co-pilot before Israeli passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker.
In a video call with India's prime minister, the Indian captain of the plane tells him
from a hospital bed in the UAE that he managed to open the cockpit door while being attacked.
The plane made an emergency landing Wednesday morning in Tabuk, where both pilots were hospitalized
for injuries.
Netanyahu says the pilot who attacked the plane's captain is from Oman.
This has yet to be confirmed by Emirati-Saudi or Omani authorities.
Ayyabhatrawi and Pierre News, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
In its latest employment reports, the Labor Department says only 29,000 jobs were created
last month.
That's far fewer than was expected.
Time is running out to register to vote in the midterm elections.
NPR's Hansi Luang has a rundown of upcoming deadlines.
The window closes this weekend for registering to vote or updating your registration in Alaska,
Rhode Island, South Carolina, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Monday, October 5, is a voter registration deadline for American Samoa, Arizona, Indiana,
and Ohio.
Monday is also the last day to sign up in many southern states, including Arkansas,
Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Texas.
Then, in Missouri, voter registration closes on Wednesday, October 7.
You can confirm your registration status by visiting your state's official election website
before the deadline.
Election officials can remove your name from voter rolls, especially if you recently moved,
changed your name, or haven't voted in a while.
Hansi Luang, NPR News.
The Trump administration is fighting a judge's order to build thousands of housing units for
homeless veterans in Los Angeles, and Pierre's Quill Lawrence has more.
L.A. has the most homeless vets in the country, but it also has a built-in solution.
A 388-acre VA campus.
A judge ordered housing to be built there, but VA appealed and lost at the Ninth Circuit
Court.
Now the Trump administration has won a delay while it considers appealing to the Supreme
Court.
The delay means no decision until after midterm elections.
Mark Rosenbaum represents the plaintiffs.
The net result is that some 3,000 veterans, including combat veterans, are going to live
and die on the meanest streets of this community.
The VA declined to comment on pending litigation.
In May 2025, President Trump ordered a 6,000-bed facility to be built in L.A., but there's
no sign of action on his executive order.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The group of seven industrialized nations says it will release 100 million barrels of
fuel over four months.
The G7 said today it'll start with a release of diesel fuel.
President Trump had announced similar news earlier today.
Trump earlier demanded that Europe distribute its stockpile as diesel costs soar in the
U.S.
The costs are due to President Trump's war in Iran, but President Trump said he would
ban U.S. diesel exports to Europe if the Europeans refused his demand.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul says she's appointed a special prosecutor to examine
allegations of rape at Cornell University.
She says the university has failed the woman who reported her assault.
Two new contenders have joined the ranks for world's loudest bird, the bear-throated bellbird
and the red-legged Sarajema, and Pierre's Ari Daniel has more.
Researchers have long studied the pitch and rhythm of bird vocalizations, but technology
now allows the measurement of volume, while a Ph.D. student at UMass Amherst, João Menezes,
and his advisor, managed to record the volume of 123 bird species across western Massachusetts
and Brazil, many for the first time.
Even in your backyard, you feel like an early naturalist.
The range was staggering, an 800-fold difference between the softest species, a kind of hummingbird,
all the way up to a very loud trio of species.
Comparable to the level of a jackhammer.
Larger species, and those with wider mouth openings, tend to sing louder, but it's still
not clear what's driving all the variety.
Ari Daniel, NPR News.
This is NPR.
